core_principles.text: The forward lunge movement strategy can be altered after ACL injury and reconstruction, characterized by a reduced contribution of the knee extensors and an increased contribution of the hip extensors.
An altered movement strategy during a forward lunge, where knee extensor contribution is reduced, is associated with knee extensor muscle weakness.

common_mistakes.text: Compensating during a forward lunge by reducing the contribution of the knee extensors and increasing the contribution of the hip extensors.

specific_findings.text: Knee extensor muscle strength declined after ACL reconstruction by 29% (p = 0.0002).
Both knee extensors (p < 0.0001) and flexors (p = 0.027) were weaker in patients post-ACL reconstruction compared to healthy controls.
The study analyzed 12 patients with an ACL injury (tested pre and ~11 months post ACL reconstruction) and 15 healthy controls.

ACL injured patients had an altered movement strategy in the forward lunge with reduced knee extensors contribution and increased hip extensor contribution compared to the controls both before and after the reconstruction.

consequences.text: An altered lunge strategy with reduced knee extensor contribution can mask underlying knee extensor weakness and joint functional deficits, potentially complicating recovery monitoring.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 1/15]

core_principles.text: Perform the forward lunge by taking one step forward, placing the foot down, and flexing the front knee to approximately 90 degrees.
Keep the upper body perpendicular to the ground during the lunge.
Place the hands on the back of the head during the lunge to control upper body motion and standardize the movement.
Maintain contact with the ground with the opposite foot during the lunge.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 12 ACL-injured patients and 15 controls, the standardized forward lunge protocol required flexing the front knee to approximately 90 degrees while keeping the upper body perpendicular to the ground.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 3/15]

core_principles.text: Maintain stable knee alignment by minimizing mediolateral knee movement or wobble during the forward lunge.
Keep the pelvis level and minimize lateral hip movement or pelvic drop during the execution of the lunge.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knee to collapse inward into valgus during the forward lunge.
Experiencing knee wobble or excessive side-to-side movement of the knee during the lunge.
Allowing pelvic drop or excessive lateral hip movement during the movement.
Compensating for weak knee extensors or knee injury by shifting the work demand to the hip joint, resulting in an increased hip joint contribution.

specific_findings.text: Knee valgus was observed in approximately 1/3 of all participants during the forward lunge.
Pelvic drop was observed in between 1/5 and 1/2 of the participants during the lunge.
Peak knee extensor moment did not change from ACL-deficient to ACL-reconstructed states but was significantly lower at both time points compared to controls, by 22% and 30%, respectively.
Peak positive knee extensor power was 49% lower in ACL-deficient and 46% lower in ACL-reconstructed patients compared to healthy controls.
Knee extensor strength was negatively correlated with the hip contribution to positive work in the ACL-deficient (r = 0.612, p = 0.034) and ACL-reconstructed (r = 0.624, p = 0.030) groups.
Knee wobble decreased by 26% and lateral hip movement decreased by 22% from pre- to post-ACL reconstruction.
Ground contact time of the lunge was 35% longer for ACL-deficient patients compared to healthy controls.

consequences.text: Knee valgus and excessive side-to-side knee movement during the lunge raise concern regarding the potential increased risk of a knee injury.
Deficits in knee extensor strength or knee joint function force a compensatory increase in hip joint contribution to perform the work during the forward lunge.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 7/15]

core_principles.text: During a forward lunge, visual kinematics such as joint angles can appear normal even when a lifter is using an altered kinetic strategy to compensate for knee extensor weakness.

common_mistakes.text: Compensating for knee extensor deficits by over-relying on the hip extensors to perform the mechanical work of the lunge.

specific_findings.text: Healthy controls exhibited a peak knee extensor moment of 1.1 plus or minus 0.1 Nm/kg during the forward lunge, which was significantly higher than the 0.8 plus or minus 0.3 Nm/kg in ACL-deficient and 0.7 plus or minus 0.2 Nm/kg in ACL-reconstructed patients.

Peak positive knee extensor power was significantly lower in ACL-deficient (2.0 plus or minus 1.3 W/kg) and ACL-reconstructed patients (2.1 plus or minus 1.6 W/kg) compared to healthy controls (3.9 plus or minus 1.4 W/kg).

ACL-reconstructed patients demonstrated a higher peak hip extensor moment of 2.3 plus or minus 0.3 Nm/kg compared to ACL-deficient patients (2.0 plus or minus 0.3 Nm/kg) and healthy controls (2.1 plus or minus 0.3 Nm/kg).

Peak positive hip joint power was significantly lower in ACL-deficient patients (4.4 plus or minus 1.5 W/kg) compared to ACL-reconstructed patients (5.6 plus or minus 1.4 W/kg) and healthy controls (5.5 plus or minus 1.8 W/kg).

consequences.text: Shifting the mechanical workload from the knee to the hip extensors reduces the loading and mechanical work performed by the knee extensors, which can prevent the normalization of knee extensor strength after ACL injury or reconstruction.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 8/15]

core_principles.text: A forward lunge requires coordinated mechanical work contributions from the hip, knee, and ankle joints during both the eccentric (negative) and concentric (positive) phases.
Knee extensor strength is a key determinant of joint work distribution, with weaker knee extensors correlating to an increased reliance on the hip joint during the concentric phase of the lunge.
Maintaining lower limb stability during a forward lunge involves controlling and minimizing mediolateral knee movement (wobble) and lateral movement of the hip.

common_mistakes.text: Compensating for knee weakness or injury by reducing knee joint contribution and excessively increasing hip joint contribution during the lunge.
Allowing mediolateral knee movement (knee wobble) and lateral movement of the hip during the execution of the lunge.

specific_findings.text: Healthy controls exhibit a positive work contribution of 47 ± 8% from the hip, 34 ± 7% from the knee, and 19 ± 7% from the ankle during a forward lunge.
Healthy controls exhibit a negative work contribution of 50 ± 8% from the hip, 35 ± 8% from the knee, and 15 ± 4% from the ankle during a forward lunge.
Patients post-ACL reconstruction demonstrated a significantly lower knee joint contribution to positive work (23 ± 11% vs 34 ± 7% in controls) and negative work (27 ± 5% vs 35 ± 8% in controls).
Patients post-ACL reconstruction compensated for reduced knee work by increasing hip joint contribution to positive work to 58 ± 10% (compared to 47 ± 8% in controls).
A significant negative correlation was observed between knee extensor strength and hip contribution to positive work during the forward lunge.

consequences.text: Reducing knee joint contribution and increasing hip joint contribution shifts the mechanical workload away from the knee quadriceps to the hip musculature, masking persistent knee extensor deficits.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 9/15]

core_principles.text: During a forward lunge, quadriceps muscle forces increase ACL loading, while the hamstrings can act to reduce these loads.
A lunge movement strategy utilizing lower knee extensor moments and lower quadriceps forces may help with unloading the ACL.

specific_findings.text: ACL-injured patients demonstrated a lower contribution of knee joint work to total lower limb work during both the negative (eccentric) and positive (concentric) work phases of a forward lunge compared to healthy controls.
Peak knee extensor moment was smaller in ACL-injured patients during the forward lunge compared to healthy controls, despite performing the movement with comparable kinematics.
A negative correlation was observed between knee extensor muscle strength and hip joint contribution to work during the lunge.
Objective analysis detected an average reduction in lateral hip movement of approximately 1 cm.

consequences.text: Increased quadriceps muscle forces increase loading on the ACL during functional tasks like the lunge.
Deficits in hamstring muscle strength, such as those resulting from an ACL reconstruction with a hamstring graft, reduce the capacity to unload the ACL via hamstring muscle forces.

source: data\lunge\Altered movement strategy during functional movement after an ACL injury, despite ACL reconstruction.pdf [part 10/15]
